prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world each placement lands 4 columns to the right of the chosen anchor, wrapping around: a brick chosen at column x lands at column (x + 4) mod 8, in the same row. The valid-action mask is in the agent's own action terms. The designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet. The starting architecture scored 0.000 on dev. That matches the 6 earlier worlds where every trial scored 0. The starting net hard-codes footprint pooling and top-left anchors, and it never reads the mask. Its zero therefore can't tell a hard task apart from a world that deviates from its description. So far the evidence rules out only one thing: a plain description-faithful net does not work with the default recipe. As the program says for round 1, all six candidates share the reference trunk and recipe. Each one changes what the net assumes about the action layout or the input layout. They also share one safeguard: if n_place is a multiple of Y*X, the mask is reshaped into K = n_place/(Y*X) maps, so a different action count (extra heights or rotations) still works. Otherwise the mask is embedded with a Linear layer. All recipes are the same, so differences between candidates come from structure. Any nonzero training success will show which hedge matters.

### Round 2
The spec matches its description. The parameter count of r1c1 (53,130) works out to K=4 types on a 64-cell grid, one DONE action and 27 obs channels (Z=6). So the action count, grid size and DONE count are as described. Round 1 also failed with all 16 action orderings, DONE-first, and channels-last or transposed obs views. A permutation of obs channels cannot be the cause either, because the 1x1 learned stem does not depend on channel order. That leaves two explanations: a deviation in dynamics or reward, which only learning can absorb, or the task is simply hard at this budget. This round therefore bets on the network's inductive bias plus how fast it learns:
- learned min/max pooling over brick windows (landing height);
- global context;
- a learned cell remap, for obs-to-action mappings that are not grid symmetries;
- more samples (1 PPO epoch);
- longer-horizon credit.

Each candidate keeps a hedged layout, and none is recipe-only.

### Round 3
After 12 trials, every dev and training score is 0. These deviations are ruled out as the only cause: action layout under all 8 symmetries and type order, DONE at index 0, anchors or footprints within a 5x5 window, obs memory views, a learned cell remap, slow learning (up to 420k steps), long-horizon credit, and window pooling or global context on the reference trunk. The 1x1 stem already absorbs any obs channel permutation. Untested so far: (a) obs scale or offset that destabilises unnormalised trunks; (b) action indices that are not any grid symmetry, or that list only valid anchors (n_place ≠ K·Y·X), which the old fallback handled with a slow dense head; (c) the value loss corrupting a shared trunk under a changed reward; (d) the hedge's summed wrong-layout maps drowning the signal; (e) dynamics that need distant context. Every file now detects a compact valid-anchor layout. Each candidate tests one of (a)-(e), plus one combined run.

### Round 4
All 18 trials scored exactly 0 on dev and in training, so no signal has appeared yet. The results rule out several deviations: action layouts under any of the 8 grid symmetries, in either type order; DONE at index 0; anchor offsets within 2 cells; memory reinterpretations of the obs; input scaling (GroupNorm); slow learning (up to 420k steps); long-horizon credit; a shared critic; distant-cell dynamics (dilation plus global context); and cell permutations that a learned remap or dense head could find. One possibility is left open: the obs groups might be misaligned with each other, or with the actions, by a symmetry other than those already hedged. Others are wrap-around (toroidal) footprints, which zero-padded convs cannot see, and vertical (3D) structure that the 2D stem misses. A reward or dynamics deviation that no net could fix is also possible. This is the last round, so each candidate makes a structural bet. Two of them are combined hedges, to maximise the chance that any run leaves zero.

## Trial it ended with
name: Two-sided symmetry kitchen sink
hypothesis: Hedges on both sides at once: the obs under all 8 symmetries, 8 output and mask layouts, both DONE positions, circular padding, GroupNorm and global context. Trains with 1 PPO epoch, entropy 0.01 and gamma 0.95. If several deviations are present together (an obs-group misalignment plus an action-layout or edge deviation), each single-change run fails, but this one could leave zero.
